=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Preliminary point: the "Reviewer Efficiency Note"

The Seller's note says clauses marked [STANDARD] "have been reviewed and cleared by both sides", and that the Buyer has "already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package". **We have not treated that as binding, and I recommend you don't either.**

- It comes from the counterparty and favours the Seller. Nearly every substantive position is tagged [STANDARD], and nothing is tagged [OPEN]. In effect it asks us not to review the deal.
- Several [STANDARD] items contradict the Seller's own Disclosure Letter:
  - Bluefen is described as "addressed", but DL §2 says no consent has been obtained.
  - Riverlark is described as "addressed", but DL §3 says the facility is unrepaid and the security is undischarged.
- **Action:** Check the internal negotiation record for any genuine agreement on these points. Unless one exists, reply that every clause stays open. Also ask for the full SPA draft. We have only the Seller's summary, so the actual clause wording must be checked.

I have reviewed everything below on its merits.

---

## A. Limitation package: structural issues (highest priority)

### 1. "Limitations apply to all Claims of any nature" (cl. 12.3/13, 9.3/12.8/20.5)
This default means the 20% cap, the thresholds and the 18-month limit would also apply to fraud, fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities. Any carve-out we negotiate elsewhere would be undermined unless it is "expressly stated".

**Push back:** Reverse the default. Limitations should apply only to general Warranty Claims. Expressly carve out:
- fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment (by the Seller, its officers or advisers)
- Fundamental Warranties
- the Tax Warranties and Tax Indemnity
- all specific indemnities

The non-reliance and exclusive-remedy clauses (9.3, 20.5) must carve out fraud. Misleading or deceptive conduct claims under s 18 of the Australian Consumer Law cannot be excluded by contract. Even so, a non-reliance clause can weaken our evidence on reliance, so the carve-out should be express.

### 2. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties capped at 20% for 18 months
This is not market practice, and "administrative simplicity" is not a reason. If title fails, we lose the entire AUD 24m, but recovery would be limited to AUD 4.8m.

**Push back:** Cap at 100% of the price (plus costs). Allow at least 6–7 years for claims, or the statutory limitation period. No de minimis or basket.

### 3. Tax "settled under the general regime"
**Push back:** Require a standalone Tax Indemnity covering pre-Completion tax, including payroll tax and superannuation guarantee charge. It should:
- cover the 100% cap
- run until the later of the ATO/state amended-assessment periods plus a buffer (typically 4–7 years)
- sit outside the de minimis and basket

### 4. Financial limits (cl. 12.1, 12.2)
- **Cap of 20% (AUD 4.8m):** Arguable for general warranties. We could accept it as a trade-off if the carve-outs above are secured, or seek 25–30%. Consider W&I insurance.
- **Basket of AUD 250k (about 1.04%), "excess only":** This is high and deductible-style. Seek 0.5% (about AUD 120k) on a tipping, first-dollar basis.
- **De minimis of AUD 25k:** Acceptable, but only if related claims or claims arising from the same facts are aggregated. This matters for the three linked Sandbar renewals (item C4).
- **18 months:** Seek 24 months, so the period covers at least two audit cycles.

### 5. Disclosure (Schedule 7 / DL §1.1–1.2) combined with Buyer knowledge (cl. 8.3)
These two provisions work together, and together they could largely neutralise the warranties:
- DL §1.1 discloses everything in the entire data room. DL §1.2 adds the statutory registers and all publicly searchable records.
- Cl. 8.3 then bars claims for anything the Buyer or its advisers knew, or that was "discoverable" from the data room or public records. That is a constructive-knowledge test.

**Push back:**
- Allow specific disclosure only, fairly disclosed with enough detail for the Buyer to assess the nature and scope of the matter.
- Data-room documents count only if expressly referenced in the Disclosure Letter.
- Public records count only to the extent of named searches run by a stated date.
- No general disclosure against Fundamental Warranties, Tax, or the specific indemnities.
- Delete cl. 8.3, or limit it to the actual knowledge of named Buyer deal-team individuals of matters fairly disclosed. Remove "advisers" and "discoverable". Ideally, include an express statement that the Buyer's knowledge does not affect claims.
- Specific indemnities must apply regardless of disclosure. Otherwise the items below are disclosed away.

DL §1.4 (non-admission) is acceptable in principle. It must not, however, weaken the "fairly disclosed" standard.

### 6. Stale disclosure date
The disclosures are made as at 22 September 2026, and today is 5 November 2026.

**Push back:** Require an updated Disclosure Letter. Any disclosure made after signing should not cure breaches of warranties given at signing; it should only give us a right to walk away. Warranties should be repeated at Completion.

---

## B. Issues requiring specific protection (from the Disclosure Letter)

### 1. Bluefen consent (DL §2; cl. 3/6.3)
- **Why it matters:** Bluefen is about AUD 3.6m, or roughly 30%, of FY26 revenue. Change of control triggers consent under cl. 11.2, which carries conditions under cl. 11.3. No consent exists, and there is no evidence those conditions are met.
- **Problem with the Seller's position:** Reasonable endeavours plus "satisfied on delivery of written consent" means a consent subject to onerous conditions (repricing, a shorter term, new termination rights) would still satisfy the Condition Precedent (CP).
- **Push back:**
  - Make this a CP: an unconditional written consent from Bluefen, or one on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, with all cl. 11.3 conditions satisfied.
  - The CP should be for the Buyer's benefit, and only the Buyer can waive it.
  - The Seller should use best endeavours, and the Buyer should have the right to review drafts.
  - Include a sunset date and a walk right.
  - Consider a price adjustment or earn-out if Bluefen terms change.
  - Add a warranty that Bluefen has not given notice of termination or non-renewal.

### 2. Riverlark facility of about AUD 3.2m (DL §3; cl. 2/7)
- **Problem:** A release "to be provided following Completion" is inconsistent with the debt-free basis. The change-of-control clause (cl. 8.1) is likely to be triggered at Completion, which could cause a default. Security would remain over Company assets, and possibly over the shares, after we own the business.
- **Push back:**
  - Repayment at Completion from the purchase price, under a payoff letter.
  - Executed deed of release, PPSR discharges and return of title documents as Completion deliverables.
  - Treat the full payout figure, including break costs and accrued interest, as Debt in the price mechanics.
  - Seek a specific indemnity.
  - Confirm whether any security is held over the Sale Shares (see C1).

### 3. DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420k (DL §5; funds flow)
- **Problem:** These bonuses are liabilities of the Company, not "a matter for the Seller". If they are left out of the funds flow, we effectively pay for them. Payroll tax, superannuation, PAYG withholding and other on-costs are not addressed.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat the bonuses plus all on-costs as Transaction Costs or Debt, deducted from the price.
  - Pay them through Company payroll at Completion, funded by the Seller, with withholding applied.
  - Add a specific indemnity, including for any bonus-related claims from employees who leave.
  - Show the bonuses as a separate line in the funds flow.

### 4. Ironquay SOW3 IP (DL §4; cl. 11.1)
- **Problem:** Under DD-004 cl. 7.3, ownership of the SOW3 Project Materials passes only once every SOW3 fee has been paid in cleared funds. DD-010 shows AUD 180k still open, and there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. The Company may therefore not own IP it relies on. An indemnity limited to "the SOW3 payment" covers the fee, not the exposure from non-ownership: infringement, inability to use or commercialise the IP, and remediation.
- **Push back:**
  - Require these Completion deliverables: evidence the AUD 180k has been paid and cleared, and an executed confirmatory IP assignment from Ironquay.
  - Alternatively, hold a retention.
  - Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own the SOW3 IP, including third-party claims. It should sit outside the cap, thresholds and time limits.
  - Diligence point: confirm how important the SOW3 materials are to the product.

### 5. DD-006 export/privacy incident (DL §6; cl. 4.6/Sch. 6)
- **Why it matters:** About 1,240 records of personal information were sent to an unintended external recipient. The investigation is still "preliminary". It is unknown whether anyone accessed the data, what the full scope is, or whether the matter must be notified.
  - Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme in Part IIIC of the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), the Company must assess a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days.
  - The incident pre-dates 22 September. The assessment window has therefore probably passed, which is a compliance risk in its own right.
  - The financial consequences could include OAIC enforcement under the enhanced civil penalty regime, customer claims, and contractual or reputational loss, possibly including with Bluefen.
- **The Seller calling it "not expected to be material" is not a basis for accepting it.**
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion: a completed forensic or investigation report, a documented NDB assessment, and evidence of any notifications to the OAIC and affected individuals.
  - Add a pre-Completion covenant giving the Buyer consultation rights on the response.
  - Add a specific indemnity for all loss from the incident, regardless of disclosure. It should sit outside the general cap, thresholds and 18-month limit, with a separate cap of at least a meaningful amount and a retention or escrow.
  - Add privacy and data warranties.

---

## C. Other points

1. **Title (DL §10).** The Company's own register at DD-012 is not enough on its own. Require:
   - a current ASIC company extract
   - share certificates and the constitution
   - a check for pre-emption rights or waivers
   - a PPSR search over the Seller and the Sale Shares (relevant to Riverlark)
   - an unlimited, long-dated title warranty that the shares are free of encumbrances.
2. **Office lease (DL §7).** Verify DD-007 ourselves. If only notice is required, make giving that notice a Completion deliverable or a post-Completion covenant, and confirm there is no "deemed assignment on change in control" provision.
3. **Mossvale (DL §9).** Check whether the assignment restriction defines "assignment" to include a change in control. If it is ambiguous, get a comfort letter or consent.
4. **Sandbar renewals (DL §8; Seller update).** These are three renewals of AUD 110k each from a single supplier, and the Seller itself says they should be read together. Check whether they were split to fall under a conduct-of-business consent threshold or a materiality threshold. If so, that is a potential covenant breach and a reason to tighten the definition of "related transactions". Obtain the contracts and check whether they can be terminated and whether amounts are accrued. Treat any non-ordinary-course commitment as Debt or cover it with an indemnity. Make sure the de minimis aggregates related claims.
5. **DL §11 (reservation).** The Seller expressly makes no assertion about whether consents or approvals are needed. That reinforces the need for warranties and CPs rather than reliance on the disclosure.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| # | Issue | Seller position | Buyer response |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | [STANDARD] labels | "Pre-agreed; don't review" | Reject. All clauses open; request full SPA draft |
| 1 | Scope of limitations | Apply to all Claims | Apply to general warranties only; carve out fraud, fundamentals, tax, indemnities |
| 2 | Fundamental warranties | 20% / 18 months | 100% of price; 6–7 years; no thresholds |
| 3 | Tax | General regime | Standalone tax indemnity; 100% cap; amended-assessment period plus buffer |
| 4 | Cap / basket / de minimis / time | 20% / AUD 250k excess / AUD 25k / 18 months | Cap negotiable; basket about 0.5% tipping; aggregate related claims; 24 months |
| 5 | Disclosure + Buyer knowledge | Whole data room + registers; constructive knowledge | Specific, fair disclosure only; delete or narrow cl. 8.3 to actual knowledge of named individuals |
| 6 | Disclosure date | 22 Sept 2026 | Updated letter; repeat warranties at Completion; later disclosure gives walk right only |
| 7 | Bluefen (about 30% of revenue) | Reasonable endeavours; any written consent | Buyer-only CP for unconditional consent with cl. 11.3 conditions met; best endeavours; sunset and walk right |
| 8 | Riverlark (about AUD 3.2m) | Release after Completion | Repaid at Completion from price; payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges as deliverables |
| 9 | Bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs) | Excluded from funds flow | Deduct as Transaction Costs/Debt; pay via payroll; indemnity |
| 10 | Ironquay SOW3 IP | Indemnity limited to fee | Payment evidence plus confirmatory assignment as deliverables; broad uncapped IP indemnity |
| 11 | DD-006 privacy incident | "Not material" | Completed investigation and NDB assessment before Completion; uncapped/separate specific indemnity; retention |
| 12 | Title | Share register only | ASIC, PPSR and certificates; unlimited title warranty |
| 13 | Sandbar, lease, Mossvale | Ordinary course / no consent | Verify; check for threshold-splitting; aggregate claims; notices as deliverables |

**Proposed next step:** Send a response that:
- states expressly that the Buyer does not accept the [STANDARD] categorisation or any "accepted framework"
- requests the full SPA draft and an updated Disclosure Letter
- puts forward the positions above.

Separately, model the price impact of items 8–11, roughly AUD 3.8m or more of identified exposure before the privacy and IP contingencies, and assess whether W&I insurance is worth pursuing alongside these protections.

1. **Title (DL §10).** The Company's own register at DD-012 is not enough on its own. Require:
   - a current ASIC company extract
   - share certificates and the constitution
   - a check for pre-emption rights or waivers
   - a PPSR search over the Seller and the Sale Shares (relevant to Riverlark)
   - an unlimited, long-dated title warranty that the shares are free of encumbrances.
2. **Office lease (DL §7).** Verify DD-007 ourselves. If only notice is required, make giving that notice a Completion deliverable or a post-Completion covenant, and confirm there is no "deemed assignment on change in control" provision.
3. **Mossvale (DL §9).** Check whether the assignment restriction defines "assignment" to include a change in control. If it is ambiguous, get a comfort letter or consent.
4. **Sandbar renewals (DL §8; Seller update).** These are three renewals of AUD 110k each from a single supplier, and the Seller itself says they should be read together. Check whether they were split to fall under a conduct-of-business consent threshold or a materiality threshold. If so, that is a potential covenant breach and a reason to tighten the definition of "related transactions". Obtain the contracts and check whether they can be terminated and whether amounts are accrued. Treat any non-ordinary-course commitment as Debt or cover it with an indemnity. Make sure the de minimis aggregates related claims.
5. **DL §11 (reservation).** The Seller expressly makes no assertion about whether consents or approvals are needed. That reinforces the need for warranties and CPs rather than reliance on the disclosure.
